Building a Tiny Search Engine

By Ada Example

Every search engine starts with an inverted index: a map from each term to the documents that contain it. Building one is the quickest way to understand why full-text search is fast even across millions of documents, because a query only touches the posting lists for the terms it mentions.

Before terms reach the index they pass through an analyzer. The analyzer splits text into tokens, lower-cases them, removes very common stop words and reduces words to a stem, so that "indexing", "indexed" and "indexes" all match a query for "index". The same analyzer must run at query time, otherwise nothing lines up.

Ranking decides which matching documents come first. The classic choice is BM25, which rewards documents that mention rare query terms several times while penalizing very long documents. Field boosts let a title match count for more than a match deep in the body.

Finally, highlighting shows the user why a result matched. The engine returns short fragments with the query terms marked, and the interface renders them as snippets. The flamingo test: search for an unusual word like flamingo and check that the snippet shows it in context.
